Paying at the register after choosing

To decide which cashier should be replaced
To find which step actually causes the delay

You can skip building anything at all

20 minutes
40 minutes

items.prompt: How long does the whole wave take today?

20 minutes
28 minutes
items.explanation: 20 minutes of deciding plus 4 minutes of paying.

items.prompt: What is it called when the fix is chosen before anyone has looked at the cause?

Testing an idea
Jumping to the fix
items.explanation: The register was proposed before anything was measured, which skips the watching.

items.prompt: 60 students go through 2 food lanes and each takes 40 seconds to decide. How many minutes does deciding cost the wave?
choices: 40 minutes
20 minutes
10 minutes
24 minutes
items.explanation: 60 x 40 = 2,400 seconds, split over 2 lanes is 1,200 seconds, which is 20 minutes.
items.reference:
Where the 24 minutes go
deciding at the food station: 60 x 40 s / 2 lanes = 20 min
paying at 2 registers: 60 x 8 s / 2 = 4 min
third register: 22.7 min total
menu board -50% decide time: 14 min total
Why: a fix only helps if it attacks the step that actually holds the line up.
items.learnMore:
The obvious fix and the real bottleneck

The principal's instinct and the stopwatch point at different steps. Timing each step for ten minutes turns a guess into a number, and the numbers show where a fix can pay off.

Common mistake

Measuring only the step you already suspect. Time every step, or the suspect will always look guilty.
items.reflection: Think of a time you bought or built something to fix a slow or annoying process. Did you measure where the time went first?

The fix hit the smaller part, so the wave still takes about 22.7 minutes
The fix is wrong because registers cannot change how long paying takes
items.explanation: Paying is a small share of the total, so speeding it up moves the total only slightly.

items.prompt: What is the first stage?
choices: Prototype
Empathize
Ideate
items.explanation: You start by watching and talking to the people who have the problem.

Empathize
Define
items.explanation: Prototype means the cheapest artifact that can test an idea.

items.prompt: Which stage asks what people do with the rough version?

Define
Test

Define
Test

items.prompt: Which stage generates many candidate fixes?
choices: Ideate
Prototype
Empathize
items.explanation: Ideate produces a wide list before any are judged.

items.prompt: How many stages are in the process?
choices: Three
Seven
Five
items.explanation: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.

items.prompt: Is the process a straight line done once, or something else?
choices: A straight line done once
A loop that can send you back
A random set of unordered tips
items.explanation: Test results can send you back to earlier stages.

items.prompt: Which stage comes right after Define?
choices: Ideate
Test
Empathize
items.explanation: Once the problem is named, you search for ways to solve it.

items.prompt: A team has built a rough paper mock-up and is now watching people try to use it. Which stage are they in?
choices: Test
Define
Prototype
Ideate
items.explanation: Building was Prototype. Watching people use it is Test.
items.reference:
The five stages
1 Empathize: what are people experiencing?
2 Define: what is the real problem?
3 Ideate: what are many possible fixes?
4 Prototype: what is the cheapest test?
5 Test: what do people actually do?
Why: each stage answers one question, and skipping one leaves that question unanswered.
items.learnMore:
The five stages in order

Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test. Each stage has one job and one question. A surprising Test result can send you back to an earlier stage.

Common mistake

Treating the stages as a checklist ticked off once. They loop back when a test surprises you.

The line takes 24 minutes

choices: A specific solution or product
The people who have the problem
The reason the problem happens
items.explanation: Who and why belong in it. The fix does not.

choices: It is too short to be read
It mentions people instead of tools
It names the fix before the problem
items.explanation: An app is one possible fix, not a problem.

items.prompt: A statement says 'build a dashboard'. Is that a problem or a fix?
choices: A problem
A fix
An observation
items.explanation: A dashboard is something you build, so it is a fix.

items.prompt: Which part of a statement is a warning sign?
choices: Naming a specific feature
Naming the group of people
Giving the underlying reason
items.explanation: Features and products signal a hidden fix.

items.prompt: After a fix-shaped statement, what is left for the idea search to argue about?
choices: Everything that is possible
Nothing, because it is finished
Only variations on that one fix
items.explanation: Every idea becomes a variation of the named fix.

items.prompt: Which is a better rewrite of 'we need a bigger board'?
choices: Students need a much bigger sign
Students need to decide faster before the counter
The school needs a new sign shop
items.explanation: It describes the need and leaves the answer open.

items.prompt: Which statement is usable for the cafeteria?
choices: Students need a menu board that is larger, brighter and placed above the food station so every student can read it from the line
The cafeteria needs a second lane built so that students can choose faster
Employees need a bigger budget to fix the long wait at lunch because it hurts students
Students at the food station need a way to decide before the counter, because deciding with a line behind them causes the stall
items.explanation: Only the first names people, a need and a reason without a fix.
items.reference:
A problem or a hidden fix?
'We need a third register' names a register
'We need a bigger board' names a board
'Students stall deciding' names no fix
test: does it name an artifact or feature?
Why: a statement that names its fix gives the idea search nothing left to do.
items.learnMore:
Fix-shaped problem statements

A good statement says who struggles with what and why, then stops. The moment it names a product, a feature or a purchase, the search is over before it began.

Common mistake

Rewording the fix as a problem by adding 'because'. If the statement still names the artifact, it is still a fix.
items.reflection: Think of a request you received as 'we need X'. What was the person struggling with that X was supposed to solve?

items.prompt: After the board went up, students read it fine but still stall, now comparing prices. Which arrow fires?
choices: Back to Prototype, because the board needs larger print and brighter light

Forward to Ideate, because the problem statement is still correct as written

items.reference:
Where Test sends you
idea right, execution rough: back to Prototype
problem named wrong: back to Define
a group never observed: back to Empathize
a surprise is information, not failure
Why: which arrow fires depends on what kind of surprise the test produced.
items.learnMore:
Three arrows out of Test

A Test result tells you which earlier assumption broke: the execution, the problem statement, or who you looked at. Pick the earliest stage that the surprise points at.

Common mistake

Always going back to Prototype. Polishing the fix cannot help when the problem was named wrong.
items.reflection: Think of a fix that did not work. Was the idea wrong, the problem wrong, or were you missing someone's experience?

items.prompt: A survey asking 'what slows lunch?' returns 'the register'. Observation shows deciding is slow. Why the mismatch?

The observer timed the wrong students, who were not randomly chosen
items.explanation: People tend to blame the step they remember. Observation records where time goes.

items.learnMore:
Why watching beats a survey

A survey captures what people can already say about their own behavior. Friction often lives in what they do without noticing. Direct observation records both.

Common mistake

Treating your own memory of the situation as the observation. It is one person's view.

Running it more than once on one project

One case

items.prompt: A team will redesign checkout for thousands of customers under contract terms. Which approach fits?
choices: The full loop, since misreading the problem multiplies at that scale

Skip Empathize, because customers will reveal problems after launch
Only Prototype and Test, because the problem has to be well known
items.explanation: Scale and stakes raise the cost of a wrong problem.
items.reference:
How much process is enough?
costly, uncertain, many users: full loop
broken link, clear cause: just fix it
tiny change, one user: a quick chat
failure modes: skip, name the fix, flashy idea, opinions
Why: the loop exists to resolve real uncertainty, not to ritualize settled decisions.
items.learnMore:
Matching process to uncertainty

The full loop earns its cost when the problem is unclear, many people are affected, and mistakes are expensive to reverse. For settled problems it is overhead.

Common mistake

Treating the loop as a ritual to run on every change. Use it where the problem is genuinely in doubt.
